title: The monkey and the crocodile
hook: caught mid-river, the monkey says he left his heart up in the fig tree (Jataka 208)

segments.voice: Yesterday: sammodamana, the quails who lifted the net together until they started bickering. Your line: together we lift the net.

Sometimes the trouble only shows itself halfway across. The friendly stranger isn't friendly. The deal isn't a deal. And the only way out is quick thinking. On the bank of the Ganges, the story goes, there lived a monkey, strong and clever. Tradition says it was the Buddha, in an earlier life. In the river lived a crocodile, whose wife had been watching the monkey leap through the trees. One day she said to her husband: I have a craving. I want to eat that monkey's heart.
screen: `HALFWAY ACROSS.` → `A MONKEY ON THE GANGES.` → `I WANT THAT MONKEY'S HEART.`

segments.voice: The crocodile swims up to the bank, all friendliness. Why stay on this side, eating the same old fruit? Across the river there are mango trees, jackfruit, the sweetest fruit you've ever tasted. Climb on my back, and I'll take you. That sounds wonderful, and the monkey hops on. Out in the middle of the river, the crocodile starts to sink. Water up to the monkey's knees. His chest. Hey, what are you doing? And the crocodile, sure he's won, tells the truth. My wife wants your heart. I'm going to drown you and bring it to her. The monkey can't fight. He can't swim to shore. So he laughs. Oh, friend, you should have said so! We monkeys don't keep our hearts inside us when we're out and about. We'd smash them to pieces, jumping from branch to branch. We hang them up in a tree for safekeeping. See that fig tree, with all the round fruit hanging on it? Those are our hearts. Take me back and I'll give you mine. The crocodile, not the brightest, swims back to the bank. The monkey leaps off, up into the fig tree, and calls down: you big fool. Did you really think anyone keeps his heart in a treetop? You're huge, but you have no wits at all. What makes this one lovely is where the monkey's strength came from. Not muscles. Not claws. A calm mind, in deep water, that saw a way out force could never find.
screen: `THE SWEETEST FRUIT ACROSS THE RIVER.` · `THE CROCODILE STARTS TO SINK.` · `MY HEART IS IN THE FIG TREE.` · `A CALM MIND IN DEEP WATER.` · then, large: `KEEP YOUR WITS.`

segments.voice: Pick a situation where you usually push: an argument, a negotiation, a kid who won't put their shoes on. Picture yourself in the middle of the river with it, and instead of struggling, take one slow breath and ask: what's another way out? A joke, a question, a different door; let an idea come.
Sumsumara. The crocodile who tricked the monkey into deep water, until the monkey stayed calm, said his heart was in the fig tree, and got away.
Your line: keep your wits. The crocodile was huge; the monkey was quick. That's day eighty-nine.

howItsDone: The monkey and the crocodile is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, appears in early Buddhist carving, and is found in the Panchatantra as well.

original.note: Pali: crocodile. The story is the Sumsumara Jataka.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly animal story with a trick at the end.
what it means: a lesson in keeping a clear mind in danger: wit instead of force.
what a scholar hears: Sumsumara Jataka, no. 208, with a close variant in the Vanarinda Jataka (no. 57); a version frames book 4 of the Panchatantra; carved at Bharhut.
